findings.location: Build Your Mental Model > `super` and constructor chaining, line 456
findings.quote: When a subclass declares a method with the same name as a base-class method, its version **overrides** the base one: calls on a subclass object run the subclass's version.
findings.source: IEEE 1800-2023 §8.14 (the Packet/LinkedPacket example: through a base-class handle p, `j = p.get(); // j = 1, not 2`, and 'the method needs to be declared virtual (see 8.20)'), §8.20; linked lesson polymorphism-pitfalls.mdx line 16/113 ('a non-virtual method runs the version the handle's class sees') and index.mdx line 789; spine card I-SV-1 misconception 3
findings.problem: Saying that calls on a subclass object always run the subclass's version is true only for virtual methods, or for calls made through a subclass handle. For a non-virtual method called through a base-class handle, §8.14 runs the base version even though the object is a subclass. The sentence teaches exactly the spine's misconception 3 ('a non-virtual method called through a base handle runs the derived version') and contradicts the next lesson, Polymorphism Pitfalls, and the module overview.
findings.fix: Replace with: "When a subclass declares a method with the same name as a base-class method, its version **overrides** the base one: a call through a subclass handle runs the subclass's version. (Through a base-class handle, only a `virtual` method runs the subclass's version; a non-virtual one runs the base version, §8.14, §8.20. [Polymorphism Pitfalls](/curriculum/T2_Intermediate/I-SV-1_OOP/polymorphism-pitfalls) covers this.)"

findings.location: Push Further > Expert: interview angles, line 1376
findings.quote: "A soft default never yields to a test's constraint. Give two causes." (The test's constraint is also soft with lower priority; or the test wrote `len == len`.)
findings.source: IEEE 1800-2023 18.5.13.1 (inline constraints have higher priority than the class being randomized; a derived class outranks all its superclasses); 18.5.13 (a soft constraint is discarded only when no solution satisfies it with the hard constraints)
findings.problem: The first model answer is close to impossible in the way a test normally adds constraints: an inline soft constraint and a soft constraint in a derived (test) item class both outrank the item's default, as this page's own ladder figure shows. The common real cause is that the test's constraint does not conflict with the default (for example `len < 10` against `soft len == 4`), so the default is correctly kept. As written, the answer suggests a test's soft constraint usually ranks below the item's default.
findings.fix: Replace the parenthetical with: "(The test's constraint does not actually conflict with the default, for example `len < 10` against `soft len == 4`, so the default is kept; or the test wrote `len == len`, which binds both names to the item. A test's own soft constraint loses only if it ranks lower, which an inline or derived-class constraint never does.)"

findings.location: Build Your Mental Model > Random stability, before/after table row 5 (line 631); the same claim sits in the Quick Take analogy (line 18) and the One-glance table (line 645)
findings.quote: | 5. Insert `std::randomize(n)`, a `randcase` or a `randsequence` between `a` and `s` | same | same | changes | All three draw from the process RNG, exactly like `$urandom` (rule 2), so `b` gets a later draw (rule 3) |
findings.source: IEEE 1800-2023 §18.16 (randcase "random numbers are obtained from $urandom_range()"); §18.14.2 ("Random values generated to select branches of the procedural randcase and randsequence statements")
findings.problem: For randcase the draw is guaranteed: §18.16 says it uses $urandom_range(). For randsequence the standard only says that the values used to *select branches* come from the thread RNG. A randsequence with no alternatives, no rand join and no random repeat count makes no random choice, and the standard does not say it takes a draw. How many values std::randomize() takes is also unspecified. "Exactly like `$urandom`" therefore claims more than §18.14 supports. The verdict (b changes) holds for any call that makes at least one random choice.
findings.fix: Change the Rule cell to: "Each one that makes a random choice draws from the process RNG (rule 2; randcase through $urandom_range, §18.16), so `b` gets a later draw (rule 3). How many draws a call takes is implementation-dependent, and a randsequence with no random choice may take none."

findings.location: Common pitfalls and misconceptions, line 710
findings.quote: It is not called when the call fails (§18.6.3), and even after a success it runs after the values are chosen, so it can only change state that the *next* call reads.

findings.source: IEEE 1800-2023 §18.3 ('The 4-state values (x or z) or 4-state operators (e.g., === , !== ) are illegal and shall result in an error')
findings.problem: §18.3 makes 4-state values and operators in constraints an error, but it does not say how or when a tool reports an X that turns up at run time in a 4-state state variable. Some tools issue a compile-time error, some a run-time error, and some a randomize() failure with a diagnostic. The lesson states one behaviour as certain.
findings.fix: Append: "(§18.3 makes this an error; whether your tool reports it at compile time, as a run-time error, or as a failed randomize() with a diagnostic is tool-dependent)."

findings.location: Reproducing a failure from its seed, line 654
findings.quote: Every module, thread and object has its own random number generator, and each one is seeded from its parent when it is created (§18.14.1).
findings.source: IEEE 1800-2023 §18.14.1 (each module instance, interface instance, program instance and package has an initialization RNG 'seeded with the default seed', which is implementation-dependent; dynamic threads and objects are seeded from the parent thread; static processes are seeded from the initialization RNG)
findings.problem: A module instance's initialization RNG is seeded with the default seed, not from a parent. Only threads and objects are seeded hierarchically.
findings.fix: Replace it with: "Every module instance has an initialization RNG seeded with the simulator's default seed, and every thread and object has its own RNG, seeded from its parent thread when it is created (§18.14.1)."

findings.location: Expert: Reproducing a failure from its seed after the code changed, line 1096
findings.quote: The IEEE 1800.2-2020 clause that specifies this is unverified here, so treat it as implementation behaviour.
findings.source: IEEE 1800.2-2020 §5.3.3.3 reseed() ('sets the seed of the object ensuring all objects have unique seeding values'; it does nothing when get_uvm_seeding returns 0), §5.3.3.1/§5.3.3.2, F.4.1.4.26 (UVM seeding defaults to 1, enabled); uvm-core 2020.3.1 base/uvm_object.svh:816, base/uvm_misc.svh:189

findings.location: Expert: State shared between objects, line 1117 (and table row line 1124)
findings.quote: `rand_mode(0)` on a `rand` class handle changes only the handle's mode, not the modes inside the object (§18.8). A nested object that "should be frozen" may still be randomized, or the reverse.
findings.source: IEEE 1800-2023 §18.8 ('only the mode of the variable is changed, not the mode of random variables within that object'); §18.5.8 a) (only rand handles that are active are added to the active random objects)
findings.problem: When the parent is randomized, an inactive handle does keep the nested object out of the solve (§18.5.8). The nested object is still randomized only if someone calls its own randomize() directly, because its variables are still active. 'May still be randomized, or the reverse' does not say when each case happens, and a learner may conclude that rand_mode(0) on the handle fails to freeze the object even through the parent.
findings.fix: Replace the second sentence with: "Through the parent's randomize() the nested object is skipped (§18.5.8), but its own variables stay active, so a direct call to the nested object's randomize() still changes them."

findings.location: Push Further > Expert: weights, zero denominators and counting only the cross, line 552
findings.quote: **Zero denominators:** an item or covergroup whose denominator is zero (every bin empty, every weight zero, or no items) contributes nothing; it reports 0.0 if its own weight is nonzero and 100.0 if its weight is zero (§19.11, §19.11.1, §19.11.2).
findings.source: IEEE 1800-2023 §19.11 (zero-denominator causes: all items excluded, all weights zero, no coverpoints or crosses), §19.11.1 ("If none of the bins have an associated value or transition, the denominator ... is zero")
findings.problem: In coverage talk an "empty bin" usually means a bin with no hits. Read that way, the sentence says a coverpoint with no hits drops out of the covergroup average. That is false: a coverpoint whose bins have no hits gives 0% and still counts in the average. The zero-denominator case in §19.11.1 is a coverpoint in which no bin has any value or transition left, for example after ignore_bins. The parenthesis also mixes the coverpoint cause with the covergroup causes.
findings.fix: Replace the parenthesis and the sentence with: "**Zero denominators:** a coverpoint none of whose bins has any value or transition left (for example, after ignore_bins), a cross with no countable bins, or a covergroup whose items are all excluded, whose weights are all zero or that has no items, has a zero denominator. It contributes nothing to the level above it, and it reports 0.0 if its own weight is nonzero and 100.0 if its weight is zero (§19.11, §19.11.1, §19.11.2). A coverpoint whose bins simply have no hits is not this case: it reports 0% and still counts."

findings.location: Practice & Reinforce > Retrieval quiz, question 5 (line 741); also Make It Work > Debugging the loop, row 3 (line 572)
findings.quote: The loop body begins: t.corner_mode = corner_mode; t = new(); if (!t.randomize()) ... What is wrong?" ... "The knob is written to the previous object; t = new() then creates an object whose corner_mode is 0, so the steering constraint never applies"
findings.source: IEEE 1800-2023 §8.4: accessing non-static members through a null object handle is illegal, the result is indeterminate, and implementations may issue an error. Lesson bench line 442: `alu_txn t;` is declared with no initializer, so it is null before the first `new()`.
findings.problem: In the bench as written, `t` is null on the first pass through the loop. A body that starts with `t.corner_mode = corner_mode;` before `t = new()` writes a member through a null handle on the first transaction. That is illegal under §8.4, and simulators normally stop with a null-object error at once. So the run cannot go on to print STEER at item 100 and then run out of budget at 10/14. The answer key's 'previous object' does not exist on the first iteration. The debugging-table row has the same gap. A learner who builds this bug to see it for themselves gets a crash, not the symptom the quiz describes.
findings.fix: Make the scenario possible. In question 5, change the prompt to: "... The bench constructs t once before the loop (alu_txn t = new();), and the loop body begins: t.corner_mode = corner_mode; t = new(); if (!t.randomize()) ... What is wrong?" Keep the answers. In the debugging table row 3, change the cause to: "The knob is set on the old handle before `t = new()` (with `t` constructed once before the loop; without that, the first write is a null-handle access, §8.4), so every new object starts with `corner_mode = 0`."

Formal tools consider every value that the assumptions and assignments allow, and simulators assign random values (§17.7.2). It may be written only by a nonblocking assignment in `always_ff`, never by a continuous or blocking assignment (§17.7.1). The free variables used below are never assigned at all, so their values are left entirely open."

findings.location: Practice & Reinforce > Retrieval quiz, Q3 option "#0 @(done);" feedback, line 923; and Push Further > Interview angles, third playground, option "Add #0 before the wait.", line 885
findings.quote: "#0 moves the wait to the Inactive region, after the Active region has run (§4.4.2.3). A trigger from the Active region at this time is then missed in every order."
findings.source: IEEE 1800-2023 §4.4.2.3 (a #0 process is resumed "in the next Inactive to Active iteration") and §4.5 (the Active region is processed again after Inactive events move to it)
findings.problem: This overstates the rule. The #0 process resumes in a later Active pass of the same time slot, not in the Inactive region. Only a trigger that runs in the current Active pass, before that resume, is certain to be missed. A trigger from a process that itself becomes active in a later pass can still be caught, or can race again. The feedback is right for the scenario these items describe (both processes ready at once), but as written it states a general rule that does not hold.
findings.fix: Quiz Q3 feedback: "#0 suspends the process until the Inactive events move back to the Active region (§4.4.2.3), so a trigger that runs in the current Active pass, such as one from a process that became ready at the same time, is missed in every order." Interview feedback: "#0 resumes the wait only after every process already in the Active region has run (§4.4.2.3). A trigger from such a process is then missed every time: the intermittent hang becomes a certain one."

findings.location: Make It Work > Debug challenge: three mutants, Mutant 1 answer (line 1168); same claim in the Where the layered bench strains debug table, row 1 (line 228)
findings.quote: **Symptom:** the first mismatch appears at an edge where a read completes and a new write arrives together (a READ followed immediately by a WRITE). From then on reads keep mismatching, and `pending` is not 0 at the end.
findings.source: The lesson's own listing: fifo_mon::run publishes a pending READ and then the current edge's observation at the same edge; fifo_sb::check. Mailbox entries are handles (IEEE 1800-2023 §15.4.3).
findings.problem: The answer key is only partly right, and the kata (line 1553) asks learners to confirm this symptom. (1) A collision also happens when a completed read is published together with a *rejected* read: a FIFO holding one item, then READ, READ. That pattern is as common as READ then WRITE in a random walk from reset. In that case the scoreboard sees the rejected READ twice and reports the mismatch at once, because model.size() is 1, not 0. (2) In the READ+WRITE case the duplicated WRITE usually passes check() at that edge, since the model is not full. The first mismatch then appears at the *next* accepted read, when the model's front still holds the lost read's data, not 'at an edge where a read completes and a new write arrives'. A learner who injects the mutant will often see a different first mismatch from the one predicted.
findings.fix: Replace the Symptom sentence with: "**Symptom:** the trouble starts at an edge where `publish` runs twice: a completed read is published together with a new write, or together with a rejected read. The first mismatch is reported either at that edge (a rejected read while the model still holds data, or a write the model thinks overflows) or at the next accepted read, whose data no longer matches the model's front. From then on reads keep mismatching, and `pending` is not 0 at the end." In the Cause sentence, change 'so the scoreboard sees the WRITE twice and never sees the READ' to 'so the scoreboard sees the second observation twice and never sees the READ'. In the debug table, row 1, change the Symptom cell to: "Mismatches start at, or soon after, an edge where a read completes together with another operation, then continue; `pending` is not 0".

findings.location: The driver's loop, 'Three rules for drivers', line 358
findings.quote: A driver's loop never finishes, so an objection raised there would never drop.
findings.source: IEEE 1800.2-2020 §10.5 (uvm_objection: raise_objection/drop_objection may be called from any component); methodology, not a rule of the standard
findings.problem: The reason given is only true for an objection raised before the forever loop. A driver that raises and drops an objection around each item would drop it. The real arguments against that are that end of test belongs to the test or top sequence, that it costs time per item, and that it lets the test end between items. As written, the claim is false for a common anti-pattern a learner may meet in legacy VIP.
findings.fix: Replace the sentence with: "A driver's loop never finishes, so an objection raised before the loop would never drop; raising and dropping one per item works, but it costs time on every item and lets the test end in the gap between items, so leave end of test to the test or the top sequence."

findings.location: Push Further > Expert: Tool and library dependence, feature table, last row (line 984); also Build Your Mental Model > What a get() can see, the paragraph under the scope-pattern table (line 223)
findings.quote: | `+` and `/…/` scope patterns | the standard says each resource's scope is a regular expression (Annex C.2.4) but leaves the matching code to the implementation | only with the DPI regular-expression code; `UVM_NO_DPI` leaves `*` and `?` |
findings.source: IEEE 1800.2-2020 C.2.4.3 ("Resource scope matching shall be determined using uvm_is_match (see F.3.3.1)"), F.3.3.1 uvm_is_match and Table F.1 (simplified notation has three meta-characters, *, + and ?; a scope in / / is a POSIX regular expression); C.4.2.2.1 set. Implementation: uvm-core 2020.3.1 src/dpi/uvm_regex.cc (glob to regex: * to .*, + to .+, ? to .) and src/dpi/uvm_regex.svh (the non-DPI fallback handles only * and ?)
findings.problem: The row says the standard leaves the pattern notation to the implementation. It does not. C.2.4.3 requires matching through uvm_is_match, and F.3.3.1 with Table F.1 defines *, + and ? and the /regex/ form as normative. So `+` and `/…/` are standard features, and losing them under UVM_NO_DPI is a limitation of uvm-core, not a choice the standard allows. The scope-pattern table and its paragraph (lines 212-223) cite only uvm-core, so a learner never sees that the notation is standard. The References list does not include F.3.3.1.
findings.fix: Replace the row's middle cell with: "yes: C.2.4.3 matches scopes with uvm_is_match (F.3.3.1), whose simplified notation is `*`, `+` and `?` (Table F.1) and whose `/…/` form is a POSIX regular expression". Replace its last cell with: "yes with the DPI regular-expression code; a library built with `UVM_NO_DPI` handles only `*` and `?`, a uvm-core limitation". At line 212 write: "A scope is a **glob**, a pattern with wildcards, matched against the whole path (IEEE 1800.2-2020 C.2.4.3, F.3.3.1, Table F.1):". At line 223 write: "The standard defines all of these forms. uvm-core implements `+` and `/…/` with C regular-expression code that it calls through DPI ...". Add "F.3.3.1 `uvm_is_match` and Table F.1 (scope notation)" to the IEEE 1800.2-2020 lines under References.

findings.location: Push Further > Expert: ending a test that has background stimulus, line 881
findings.quote: **Object from the sequence itself.** `set_automatic_phase_objection(1)` makes a sequence raise and drop the starting phase's objection around its own execution (§14.2.4.4).
findings.source: IEEE 1800.2-2020 §14.2.4.3 ("automatically raises an objection to the starting phase (if the starting phase is not null)"), §14.2.4.1 ("The starting phase is set automatically when this sequence is started as the default sequence on a sequencer"), §14.2.4.2 set_starting_phase; uvm-core 2020.3.1 uvm_sequence_base.svh:701-720 (m_safe_raise_starting_phase does nothing when get_starting_phase() is null)
findings.problem: The rule is stated without its condition. The automatic objection only works when the sequence has a starting phase. That is set automatically only for a phase's default sequence. This page starts its sequences with vseq.start(null) from the test's run_phase, and there the starting phase is null. A learner who swaps the test's raise/drop for set_automatic_phase_objection(1) gets no objection at all, so the run phase ends at time 0 and nothing is driven.
findings.fix: Replace the bullet with: "**Object from the sequence itself.** `set_automatic_phase_objection(1)` makes a sequence raise and drop its starting phase's objection around its own execution (§14.2.4.3, §14.2.4.4), but only when it has a starting phase. A phase's default sequence gets one automatically (§14.2.4.1). A sequence you start yourself, like `vseq.start(null)` here, needs `vseq.set_starting_phase(phase)` first (§14.2.4.2); otherwise nothing objects and the phase can end at once. The standard's own note warns against it for a sequence with a `forever` loop, because the objection never drops."

findings.location: Make It Work > Expected output, 'The times' bullet, line 1300
findings.quote: Reports come bottom-up, so `cov` (inside `agt`) reports before `sb`.
findings.source: uvm-core 2020.3.1 base/uvm_bottomup_phase.svh:68-75 (post-order traversal; children in get_first_child/get_next_child order, which is by name)
findings.problem: Bottom-up order alone does not put cov before sb. cov is a grandchild of env and sb is a child, but they sit in different subtrees. Each subtree finishes before its parent, and siblings go in name order. cov comes first because env's child 'agt' sorts before 'sb'. A learner would wrongly conclude that every deeper component reports before every shallower one.
findings.fix: Replace it with: "Each subtree reports before its parent, and in uvm-core siblings go in name order, so the whole `agt` subtree (`cov` included) reports before `sb`."

findings.location: Build Your Mental Model > The four driver calls compared, rule 3, line 138 (contradicts the prediction reveal at line 173 and the pitfall at line 182)
findings.quote: **`try_next_item()` never waits for a sequence to start.** It gives sequences that already asked for a grant one NBA region (one `wait_for_sequences()` call) to send an item, then returns `null`.
findings.source: Pedagogy: 'nothing is duplicated or contradictory' and an example comes before the rule it illustrates. The lesson's own prediction answer (line 173) says driver B gets the item of a sequence that calls start_item() after try_next_item() was called, and the has_do_available() pitfall (line 182) says try_next_item() 'would still serve' a sequence that calls start_item() later in the same time slot.
findings.problem: Rule 3 says the call serves only sequences that 'already asked for a grant' and 'never waits for a sequence to start'. A learner who applies it to the prediction just below (no sequence waiting when driver B calls try_next_item(); the sequence calls start_item() later in the same Active region) predicts null. The reveal then says B gets the item and does not reconcile this with the rule. The rule as worded conflicts with the lesson's own answer key and pitfall.
findings.fix: Replace the bullet with: "**`try_next_item()` never waits beyond the current time slot.** It waits for the NBA region of this time slot (one `wait_for_sequences()` call), so any sequence that has called `start_item()` by then can be granted and send its item. If none has, it returns `null` without consuming time." In the reveal's 'Why' cell for driver B, add: "(rule 3: the request only has to be queued by the NBA region, not when the call starts)".

findings.location: What happens when a library starts, 'Pitfall: an objection in pre_body()' (line 249); How to build it yourself step 2 (line 720); Retrieval quiz Q9 correct-option feedback (line 1018)
findings.quote: Put objection code in `pre_start()` and `post_start()`, which run in every start style
findings.source: IEEE 1800.2-2020 §14.2.4.1 (the starting phase is set automatically only when the sequence is started as a default sequence); uvm-core 2020.3.1 uvm_sequence_library.svh execute() and the `uvm_rand_send macro (uvm_sequence_defines.svh:155-177) call set_item_context() and start(), never set_starting_phase(); I-UVM-3A index.mdx line 468 (do objections in pre_start()/post_start() and check get_starting_phase() for null first)
findings.problem: The hooks do run, but a library member has no starting phase: get_starting_phase() returns null, because the library never passes its own phase on. The hand-written objection pattern that I-UVM-3A teaches (null-checked get_starting_phase() in pre_start()) therefore raises nothing in a member, so moving the code from pre_body() to pre_start() does not make the member object. The pitfall, build step 2 and quiz Q9 all present the move as the fix. A learner who follows them still gets no objection from the member. The run is only kept alive by the test's objection, or by the library's own objection when the library has a starting phase (uvm-core).
findings.fix: After the pitfall's last sentence (line 249) add: 'One more catch: a member has no starting phase of its own. Only a default sequence gets one automatically (§14.2.4.1), and the library does not pass its own on (uvm-core 2020.3.1 execute()), so a member's get_starting_phase() returns null and objection code in its pre_start() raises nothing either. Under a library, let the test object around lib.start(), or give the library a starting phase so it objects for the whole run (uvm-core).' Line 720: 'Put setup code in pre_start(), never in pre_body(); leave objections to the test or to the library, because a member has no starting phase.' Quiz Q9 feedback (line 1018): 'Right. pre_start() and post_start() always run, but a member also has no starting phase, so keep the objection in the test or on the library (set_starting_phase on the library) rather than in the member (B.3.1.3, §14.2.3.1, §14.2.4.1).'

findings.location: Push Further, 'Expert: libraries as phase default sequences', knobs bullet (line 779); Retrieval quiz Q7 option 3 feedback (line 996)
findings.quote: A library that a test starts without randomizing never reads them.
findings.source: IEEE 1800-2023 §18.6.2 (randomize() first invokes pre_randomize()); uvm-core 2020.3.1 uvm_sequence_library.svh lines 603-605 (pre_randomize() calls m_get_config()) and 723/741 (body() calls randomize(select_rand) or randomize(select_randc) on every pick)
findings.problem: In RAND and RANDC mode, body() calls randomize(select_rand) or randomize(select_randc) on the library object at every pick. findings.location: Practice & Reinforce > Debug challenge: the agent that never started, question 2 (line 1074) and worked answer 2 (line 1081)
findings.quote: Which one line, added in the test's `report_phase` (or just before the timeout with a short `set_timeout`), shows the cause?
findings.source: IEEE 1800.2-2020 F.7.3.2 (die: pre_abort hooks, report_summarize, then $finish) and 13.1.4.6 (pre_abort runs on a UVM_EXIT action); uvm-core 2020.3.1 src/base/uvm_phase_hopper.svh:587 (`uvm_fatal("PH_TIMEOUT", ...)) and src/base/uvm_root.svh:157-182 (die() calls m_do_pre_abort and report_summarize, never the remaining phases)
findings.problem: The scenario says the test hangs until PH_TIMEOUT. That timeout is a UVM_FATAL, and the fatal's exit action calls uvm_root::die(). die() runs the pre_abort hooks, prints the report summary and calls $finish, so check_phase and report_phase never run. A print added to report_phase therefore never appears, and the parenthetical does not say where the line should go instead. The question rests on a false premise, and a learner who follows it sees nothing.
findings.fix: Replace question 2 with: "Which one line, added in the test's `pre_abort()`, shows the cause? (`pre_abort()` runs when the PH_TIMEOUT fatal stops the run, before the summary prints. `report_phase` never runs after a fatal: IEEE 1800.2-2020 §13.1.4.6, F.7.3.2.)" Begin answer 2 with "In the test's `function void pre_abort();`, call `uvm_event_pool::get_global_pool().print();`" and keep the rest of the answer.

findings.location: Try it: why is my stream empty? line 186 (<TransactionRecordingVisualizer />); text in src/components/visuals/TransactionRecordingVisualizer.tsx line 23 and src/lib/uvm-recording-model.ts isEnabled()
findings.quote: Explorer assumption: "…until set_recording_enabled(1) (IEEE 1800.2 13.1.6.13) or a non-zero recording_detail config value read at construction/build (library behaviour)." Explorer feedback: "The driver reads recording_detail when it is constructed and built…" / "The driver read recording_detail during construction and build_phase."
findings.source: IEEE 1800.2-2020 13.1.7.13 (set_recording_enabled; 13.1.6 is a different subclause); uvm-core 2020.3.1 src/base/uvm_component.svh: uvm_component::new looks up "recording_detail" (lines ~1782-1797), and apply_config_settings in the default CONFIG_CHECK_NAMES mode (uvm_global_defines.svh) applies only names reported by do_execute_op(UVM_CHECK_FIELDS), which uvm_component does not report. Lesson lines 139 and 889-890 teach exactly this.
findings.problem: The embedded explorer contradicts the lesson. The lesson says uvm-core reads recording_detail only in the constructor, "not even by its own build_phase" (line 139, expert note line 890, quiz Q9 option 4). The explorer, which the learner uses just before that, says the setting is read at construction and in build_phase. It also cites set_recording_enabled as IEEE 1800.2 13.1.6.13, a clause number that does not exist for that method. The standard defines it in 13.1.7.13, and the lesson cites that number. The run_phase outcome agrees, but the stated reason and the citation are wrong.
findings.fix: In TransactionRecordingVisualizer.tsx RECORDING_MODEL_ASSUMPTIONS[0], write: "Follows uvm-core 2020.3.1: recording_detail defaults to UVM_NONE, so get_recording_enabled() is 0 until set_recording_enabled(1) (IEEE 1800.2 13.1.7.13) or a non-zero recording_detail config value that the component's constructor reads (uvm-core behaviour; the default CONFIG_CHECK_NAMES mode does not re-read it in build_phase)." In uvm-recording-model.ts isEnabled(), change the set_recording_enabled reason to "(IEEE 1800.2 13.1.7.13)", the config-before-build reason to "The driver reads recording_detail in its constructor, so a set made before the driver is created enables recording (uvm-core behaviour)." and the config-in-run-phase reason to "The driver read recording_detail in its constructor, during build. A set made in run_phase is never read." In the header comment, change 13.1.6.13/13.1.6.14 to 13.1.7.13/13.1.7.14 and drop "and again in apply_config_settings (build_phase)".

findings.location: Quick Take line 18; architecture section line 73; Turning recording on line 141
findings.quote: "With recording off, `begin_tr` still sets the transaction's begin time and triggers its events, but it opens no recorder and returns 0, and `end_tr` writes nothing (§13.1.7.3, §13.1.7.5)."
findings.source: IEEE 1800.2-2020 13.1.7.3: "A handle to the transaction is returned. The meaning of this handle … [is] application specific". Only the tr_handle passed to do_begin_tr is required to be 0 when recording is off (13.1.7.3 c). uvm-core 2020.3.1 m_begin_tr returns handle = 0 when get_recording_enabled() is 0.
findings.problem: The lesson presents "begin_tr returns 0 when recording is off" as the rule of §13.1.7.3. For the component's begin_tr, the standard leaves the meaning of the returned handle to the implementation. Returning 0 is uvm-core behaviour; the standard only requires the 0 that do_begin_tr receives. The lesson's rule "say uvm-core when that is the source" is not applied here.
findings.fix: At line 141, after "returns 0", insert "(uvm-core; §13.1.7.3 itself only requires do_begin_tr to receive a handle of 0, and leaves the meaning of begin_tr's return value to the implementation)". At line 73, change "`begin_tr` returns it, and 0 means \"nothing was opened\"" to "`begin_tr` returns it; in uvm-core, 0 means \"nothing was opened\"".

findings.location: Error and event records, line 323 and table lines 329-333
findings.quote: "| Duration | begin time to end time | zero: closed at the time given (0 means now) | zero, the same way |" … "| Fields come from | … | `info.record()`, if `info` is not null | `info.record()`, if `info` is not null |" … "| Returns | `begin_tr`: the handle, or 0 | 0; the handle when `keep_active = 1` | 0; the handle when `keep_active = 1` |"
findings.source: IEEE 1800.2-2020 13.1.7.7: "if 0, then a zero-length error transaction is recorded" and "A handle to the transaction is returned". 13.1.7.8 says nothing about info's properties being recorded. uvm-core 2020.3.1 uvm_component.svh record_error_tr/record_event_tr: both always call recorder.close(time), record info, and return 0 unless keep_active.
findings.problem: The rows state uvm-core behaviour as if it were the standard. The standard makes the error record zero-length only when keep_active = 0. It does not say an event record carries info's fields. It does not say the return value is 0 when keep_active = 0. Only the TYPE row and the "Written while recording is off" row are labelled uvm-core.
findings.fix: Append "(uvm-core)" to the Duration, Fields come from and Returns row labels, or add after the table: "The Duration, Fields and Returns rows describe uvm-core 2020.3.1. §13.1.7.7 requires a zero-length error record only when keep_active = 0, §13.1.7.8 does not mention recording info, and both clauses leave the returned handle's meaning to the implementation."

findings.location: Make It Work, sentence before the tr_db.log listing, line 669
findings.quote: "Handles and `inst_id` values vary."
findings.source: uvm-core 2020.3.1 src/base/uvm_recorder.svh get_handle() and src/base/uvm_tr_stream.svh get_handle(): handle = get_inst_id().
findings.problem: The illustrative log shows stream and recorder handles 1 to 13 next to item inst_id values 60 to 66.
